paras: A convention does not become law because it is adopted. What makes it law in any particular ship is ratification by the state whose flag she flies, followed by transposition into that state's own legislation. It is for that reason that two identical vessels, side by side at the same berth, may be subject to different provisions of the same instrument.

The vessel in this case was registered in a state which had ratified the convention but not the protocol that replaced its survey regime. The classification society to which the owner had contracted the surveys held an authorisation from that flag state and from no other. The port authority in whose waters she lay was acting for a state which had ratified both instruments, and whose inspectors were therefore applying a standard the ship had never been built to meet.

It was not the surveyor who was at fault, and it was not the master. What produced the detention was an amendment that one registry had accepted and the other had not, and a certificate that was valid under the law of the flag and insufficient under the law of the port. Both readings were correct. Only one of them was enforceable in that harbour.

The case is cited whenever the industry discusses jurisdiction, because it shows what compliance actually costs. Liability did not follow the fault; it followed the flag. And enforcement, which is the only part of the system the master can see from the bridge, belonged to the state that had done nothing at all except open its port.

items.situation: It was not the surveyor who was at fault. What does the sentence do that the surveyor was not at fault does not?
tips: It names the surveyor in order to exclude him, and it implies somebody else.
The it-cleft always points at one item and pushes the rest out of frame.

items.situation: The port authority in whose waters she lay was acting for a state which had ratified both instruments. Which had ratified: the authority, the waters, or the state?
tips: The state. Which attaches to the nearest suitable noun, not always the nearest word.
Re-attaching the clause is how the wrong option is built.

items.situation: Say, in exam register, that a treaty is not law just because it was agreed.
tips: Adoption alone does not give a convention legal force.
Ratification and transposition are what make it binding.

items.situation: Turn this into a wh-cleft: an amendment produced the detention.
tips: What produced the detention was an amendment.
The wh-cleft delays the important item to the end.

items.situation: Whose flag she flies. Can whose be used for a thing rather than a person?
tips: Yes. Whose works for things, states and organisations, not only for people.
That is why the state whose flag is correct and the state which flag is not.

items.situation: In one sentence, say why two identical ships at the same berth can be bound by different rules.
tips: Because their flag states ratified different instruments.
The ship is bound by what her own registry accepted, not by what the convention says.

listenings.text: I have been asked the same question by three different lawyers, and the answer has not changed. I surveyed that vessel against the regime her flag state had accepted, because that is the only regime I am authorised to survey her against. My authorisation comes from one administration and from no other. If a port on the far side of an ocean has ratified a protocol that her registry has not, that is not a defect in my survey and it is not something I am permitted to correct. What people find hard to accept is that both certificates in that argument were valid. Mine was valid under the law that appointed me. Theirs was valid under the law that controlled the water. It was the water that won, and it always is.

There are three steps and most people only know the first. A convention is adopted at the organisation, and that is the photograph everybody has seen. Then it has to be ratified, which means each state accepts to be bound by it, and the instrument only enters into force once enough of them have done so. And then, third, it has to be transposed: written into the national law of that state, with a penalty attached. A state can complete step two and never complete step three, and when that happens you have a convention that is technically in force and practically invisible. It is enforcement, not ratification, that decides what a master actually experiences. Which is why the interesting question about any flag is never what it has signed. It is what it has ever detained a ship for.
